meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 7 (Multi-Select): Authorization (OAuth 2.1)
meta.format: multi_select: questions use the 'answers' array (multiple correct options). Some include an 'All of the above' option that is only correct when every other option is.

questions.question: Authorization is optional for MCP servers, but strongly recommended when... (Select all that apply.)

options.text: the server accesses user-specific data such as emails, documents, or databases
you need to audit who performed which actions
the server grants access to APIs requiring user consent
you're building for enterprise environments with strict access controls
the server only performs pure, stateless math with no data access

questions.explanation: The tutorial lists user data, auditing, consent-gated APIs, enterprise controls, and per-user rate limiting/usage tracking as the triggers. A pure calculator has no such need.

questions.question: Order-independent: which steps are genuinely part of the MCP OAuth authorization flow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Server returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate pointing at the Protected Resource Metadata
Client fetches PRM, then the authorization server's metadata (OIDC discovery or RFC 8414)
Client registers (pre-registered, DCR, or CIMD) and sends the user to the authorization endpoint
Client exchanges the authorization code for tokens using PKCE
Client embeds the access token in the JSON-RPC id field of each request

questions.explanation: Steps A–D are the flow. Tokens travel in the Authorization: Bearer header — never in the JSON-RPC message itself.

questions.question: Which RFC/standard pairings used by MCP authorization are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: RFC 9728 — Protected Resource Metadata
RFC 8414 — Authorization Server Metadata
RFC 7591 — Dynamic Client Registration
RFC 8707 — Resource Indicators
RFC 2616 — Token introspection

questions.explanation: The four pairings are correct; RFC 2616 is the old HTTP/1.1 spec — token introspection is RFC 7662.

questions.question: Which items appear on the authorization tutorial's 'pitfalls to avoid' list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Implementing token validation logic yourself instead of using well-tested libraries
Logging Authorization headers, tokens, or secrets
Accepting generic audiences (like 'api') or unrelated resources
Tying authorization decisions to the Mcp-Session-Id header
Returning WWW-Authenticate challenges on 401 responses

questions.explanation: A–D are pitfalls (session identifiers are untrusted input; never tie authorization to them). Returning proper WWW-Authenticate challenges is a recommended practice, not a pitfall.

questions.question: Which requirements does the 2026-07-28 authorization spec place on MCP clients? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Validate a present iss parameter against the recorded issuer before redeeming the authorization code
Key persisted client credentials by issuer and never reuse them with a different authorization server
Specify an appropriate application_type during Dynamic Client Registration
Use PKCE in the authorization code flow
All of the above

questions.explanation: SEP-2468, SEP-2352, SEP-837, and the OAuth 2.1 baseline respectively — all four are real MUSTs, so 'All of the above' stands.

questions.question: Which client-registration mechanisms exist for MCP, and in what standing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Pre-registered static clients
Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) — still works, but deprecated
Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) — the recommended replacement, using a URL as the client ID
API-key self-registration defined by the MCP spec
All of the above

questions.explanation: Static registration, DCR (deprecated), and CIMD are the three; MCP defines no API-key registration scheme.

questions.question: A request hits your protected MCP server. Which response pairings are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: No token, or an expired/invalid one → 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge pointing at the Protected Resource Metadata
Valid token missing a needed scope → 403 with insufficient_scope, prompting client step-up for the scope union
Mcp-Name header contradicting the body → 400 with HeaderMismatch (-32020)
Valid token for a different audience → accept it, since the issuer matches
All of the above

questions.explanation: Audience mismatch means rejection — accepting it is the token-passthrough anti-pattern. That false D poisons the all-of-the-above option.

questions.question: Which discovery documents and standards participate in the MCP OAuth flow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728), found via the WWW-Authenticate header
Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414 or OIDC discovery)
Resource Indicators (RFC 8707) binding tokens to the target server
WSDL service descriptions
All of the above

questions.explanation: PRM → AS metadata → resource-bound token request is the discovery chain. WSDL belongs to SOAP, not OAuth.
